observatory.title: Observatory
observatory.description: A planet generated entirely in code: terrain, craters, clouds, rings and atmosphere, with no downloaded texture.
observatory.note: Everything is generated in code at load time: terrain, craters, clouds, rings and sky. No texture is downloaded.
observatory.hint: Drag to orbit · scroll to zoom

systems.title: Planetary systems
systems.description: The Solar System planet by planet, four real exoplanet systems, and systems generated on demand.
systems.generatedNote: Fictional but physically consistent: orbits follow Kepler's third law, temperatures follow the star's luminosity.
systems.scaleNote: Sizes, distances and speeds are compressed to fit the screen; the values shown are real.
systems.hintOrbit: Hover to identify · click to inspect · Space to pause
systems.hintCarousel: Scroll or ← → to browse · click or Enter to inspect
systems.hintInspect: Drag to rotate · scroll to zoom · Esc to go back
systems.starNote: Luminosity derived from radius and temperature (Stefan–Boltzmann law).
systems.generateHint: A new seed, a new system
systems.moonsLegend: Radius · distance from the planet · orbital period
systems.hintMoons: Click a moon to inspect it

credits.title: Credits
credits.description: Sources of the planetary maps and data.
credits.fontsNote: Instrument Serif, Geist and Geist Mono, via Google Fonts (SIL Open Font License).
credits.code: Everything else (procedural planets, atmospheres, rings, stars, sky, catalogue objects) is generated in code.
credits.objectsNote: Each object's figures come from the pages cited on its sheet (English Wikipedia, which links to the original publications). The 3D models, nebulae, galaxies and black-hole simulations are generated in code; only Pluto and Ceres use a real map.

objects.title: Space objects
objects.description: Black holes, pulsars, quasars, galaxies, nebulae, comets, dwarf planets and spacecraft: real examples with their known data, modelled in 3D.
objects.hint: Drag to rotate · scroll to zoom

appearance.texture: Real surface map (NASA / USGS, public domain).
appearance.simulation: Simulation: light paths and effects computed, colours and scales illustrative.
appearance.impression: Artist's view: shape and colours based on real images, procedural structure.

black-holes.name: Black holes
black-holes.blurb: Regions where gravity holds back even light. They are only seen through what surrounds them: the matter falling in and heating up, and the background starlight they bend.

neutron-stars.name: Neutron stars
neutron-stars.blurb: The collapsed cores of massive stars: more than a solar mass in a ball some twenty kilometres across. Pulsars sweep space with their beams like lighthouses.

quasars.name: Quasars
quasars.blurb: The most luminous galactic nuclei, powered by a supermassive black hole devouring gas. They outshine whole galaxies and light up the young Universe.

galaxies.name: Galaxies
galaxies.blurb: Systems of billions of stars, gas and dust. Spiral, elliptical or irregular, their shape tells their history.

nebulae.name: Nebulae
nebulae.blurb: Clouds of gas and dust: nurseries where stars are born, or the remains of those that die.

comets.name: Comets
comets.blurb: Lumps of ice and dust from the outer Solar System. Near the Sun they unfurl a coma and two tails.

dwarf-planets.name: Dwarf planets
dwarf-planets.blurb: Worlds massive enough to be round, but that have not cleared their orbit. Five are recognised by the International Astronomical Union.

spacecraft.name: Spacecraft
spacecraft.blurb: Objects humanity has sent into space: crewed stations, telescopes, probes.
